chunks: Drive an inductive load from a GPIO. The question: Design a circuit to drive an inductive load from a microcontroller GPIO.
A microcontroller pin can supply only a few milliamps at 3. 3 volts. A solenoid or relay needs hundreds of milliamps at a higher voltage.
So the pin controls a transistor switch, and the transistor carries the load current.
A coil also fights any sudden stop in its current, so you add a diode to give that current a safe path when the switch opens.
Think of a small lever that opens a big water valve: your finger only needs a tiny push. The coil is like a long, heavy pipe full of moving water.
If you slam a valve shut, the water hammers the pipe. A bypass loop lets the water keep circulating and slow down gently. The diode is that bypass loop.
The coil's stored energy ends up as heat in the coil and diode.
The flyback diode sits across the load with its cathode on the +12 volts side.
R g (100 to 220 ohms) limits the GPIO current and damps ringing; R pd (10 to 100 kilohms) keeps the gate low whenever the pin is not driving.
GPIO: a general-purpose pin on a microcontroller that you set high or low in software.
Logic-level MOSFET: a transistor switch whose control pin (the gate) turns it fully on at logic voltages such as 3. 3 volts.
Low-side switch: a switch between the load and ground, so the gate voltage is simply measured from ground.
Flyback diode: a diode across the coil that conducts when the switch opens. Gate pull-down: a resistor from gate to ground that keeps the switch off when the pin is not driving.
Drive a 12 volts solenoid with a 24 ohms coil. The current is 12 over 24 equals 0. 5 amps, far more than a pin can give.
Put a logic-level NFET between the coil and ground and connect the pin to its gate through about 220 ohms. Place a diode across the coil, cathode to +12 volts.
When the FET turns off, the coil's 0. 5 amps circulates through the diode and fades over a few milliseconds. The drain stays near 12 volts instead of spiking to hundreds of volts.
That is the whole idea.
"I'd use a low-side logic-level N-channel MOSFET: load from the supply to the drain, source to ground, GPIO to the gate.

A flyback diode across the load takes the inductive kick, a 100 k pull-down on the gate keeps it off when the MCU is in reset, a 100 to 220 ohms series gate resistor limits GPIO current and ringing, and a bulk capacitor supports the supply.
If the load is on a different or noisy supply, add isolation between the MCU and the gate."
